Going to Mars without first setting up a permanent base on the Moon is stupid. We can perfect more technology close to home, then launch our rockets from the Moon - which is WAAAAAAY easier than launching from Earth... and that means smaller, cheaper, more fuel-efficient rockets.
The moon has no atmosphere whereas mars does have one. They are different environments that we have to acclimate the spacecraft to. The two weeks of darkness on the moon is another difference.

You're still going to need a lot of the same technology in both places. No one said they were exactly the same. Besides, if the rockets have to travel through space, they'll be fine starting off in a no-atmosphere location and will already have to be ready to handle vacuum as well as Mars atmosphere.

The problem is: how do you get the fuel for the Moon-to-Mars rockets to the surface of the moon? You have to bring it from Earth, unless we are building a full-on rocket factory on the moon, using only resources we can scavenge from the moon.

A Lunar rocket factory and launch facility would require tons of infrastructure (read as: spending) to try to scavenge water from the moon (by looking for ice in shaded-craters or buried in regolith perhaps), separate O2 and H2 from the water, cool it to cryogenic temperatures and prepare it for launch. You are essentially building Kennedy Space Center on the moon, easily a multi-trillion dollar project.

In a world where funding science takes top priority, this could happen. But with congress giving NASA 18 billion while DOD gets 600-880 billion per year, that won't happen, and we're back to hauling the fuel from Earth.

In the case where we are bringing the fuel from Earth, then it's less costly (both in terms of $$$ and Delta-V) to go straight from the Earth to Mars.

There are other differences between the environments where lunar-specific requirements do not apply to Mars requirements and vice-versa (i.e. no useable atmosphere for an aero-braking descent on the moon versus a thin atmosphere for a limited-assist aero-braking descent on Mars, more-dangerous lunar regolith / dust versus less-dangerous martian soil, short-term exposure to cosmic rays on a 4-day Earth-to-moon transit versus long-term exposure on an Earth-Mars transit. Even communication latency is vastly different.

I would like to see NASA pursue both goals but without massive funding, rocket factories / interplanetary launch facilities on the moon are a long way off.
